title: "Financial Foundations — Follow the Money"

# First learn to draw money on a timeline

Finance becomes much easier once you stop memorising product names and start asking just three questions:

1. **Who pays?**
2. **How much do they pay?**
3. **When do they pay it?**

Imagine lending a friend 100 today. They promise 5 after one year and 105 after two years. This will be our **running example** throughout the fixed-income lessons. Sometimes we will change just one assumption, such as the interest rate, the payment date or the possibility of default.

## Learn in this order

1. [Cash-flow timelines](01-cash-flow-timeline.qmd) — what positive and negative flows mean.
2. [Compounding and present value](02-compounding-and-present-value.qmd) — why future money is not worth the same as current money.
3. [Net present value and internal rate of return](03-npv-and-irr.qmd) — when a project is worth paying for.
4. [No arbitrage](04-no-arbitrage.qmd) — why two ways of obtaining the same payoff should cost the same in an ideal market.
5. [Yield versus realised return](05-total-return-vs-yield.qmd) — why a quoted yield is not your guaranteed investment result.

When a chapter uses a formula, the next paragraph explains the letters and substitutes real numbers. You should be able to reproduce every calculation using a calculator.

## Source orientation

Luenberger, *Investment Science*, **2nd ed., Chapters 1–3**, treats cash flows and interest as building blocks of investment mathematics. Fabozzi (ed.), *The Handbook of Fixed Income Securities*, **8th ed., Chapters 1, 6**, brings those ideas into bond-market conventions. These lessons are independently written rather than copied from the books.
